title: The Invisible Living World
subject: Science
description: Cells and their parts, levels of organisation, and the microorganisms — bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses — that decompose waste, ferment food, fix nitrogen and make oxygen.

questions.question: Why was the curved piece of glass that magnifies things named a 'lens'?
options: It was shaped like a lentil seed
It was first ground in a town named Lens
It was made from lens-shaped river sand
It was named after its Dutch inventor
questions.explanation: The chapter says the glass was thick in the middle and thin at the edges, like a lentil seed — hence 'lens'. The other origins are not what the text gives.

questions.question: Which description matches the shape of a lens as given in the chapter?
options: Thin in the middle and thick at the edges
Thick in the middle and thin at the edges
Flat on one face and hollow on the other
Equally thick everywhere but gently curved
questions.explanation: A lens is thick in the middle and thin at the edge, just like a lentil seed. Reversing this (thin in the middle) is the common mix-up.

questions.question: In Activity 2.1, letters look larger when seen through a water-filled round-bottom flask. Why?
options: The water dissolves a little ink so letters spread
The cork traps air that pushes the letters apart
The water-filled flask behaves like a magnifying glass
The glass reflects light back towards your eyes
questions.explanation: The curved flask full of water acts like a lens (magnifying glass), bending light so the letters appear bigger. Nothing happens to the ink or the air.

questions.question: Who published the book Micrographia in 1665?
questions.explanation: Robert Hooke published Micrographia in 1665 with detailed drawings of tiny things seen through his microscope. Leeuwenhoek worked around the same time but did not write this book.

questions.question: What did Robert Hooke see when he looked at a thin slice of cork?
options: Tiny moving creatures that looked like bacteria
Many small empty spaces like a honeycomb
Green grains of pigment packed in rows
Long branched threads without any colour
questions.explanation: Hooke saw many small, empty compartments that reminded him of a honeycomb and called each one a 'cell'. Bacteria were first described by Leeuwenhoek, not Hooke.

questions.question: Which statement about Robert Hooke is NOT correct?
options: His microscope magnified about 200 to 300 times
He was a careful observer and a skilled artist
He drew what he saw in a thin slice of cork
He was the first to clearly describe bacteria
questions.explanation: It was Antonie van Leeuwenhoek who first clearly saw and described bacteria and blood cells. Hooke is known for the cork cells, Micrographia and a 200–300× microscope.

questions.question: Who is known as the Father of Microbiology?
questions.explanation: Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch scientist, built better microscopes and was the first to clearly see and describe bacteria and blood cells, so he is called the Father of Microbiology.

questions.question: Robert Hooke was the first person to use the word 'cell' in science to describe the basic unit of life.
questions.explanation: Hooke named the honeycomb-like compartments of cork 'cells'; this was the first scientific use of the word.

questions.question: Hooke's microscope magnified objects 100 to 400 times.
questions.explanation: Hooke's microscope magnified 200 to 300 times. The 100–400 times figure is given later for the microscopes used to view microorganisms in Tables 2.1 and 2.2.

questions.question: An electron microscope magnifies about 10,00,000 times. Taking Hooke's microscope as 250×, roughly how many times stronger is the electron microscope?
questions.explanation: 10,00,000 ÷ 250 = 4,000. So the electron microscope magnifies about four thousand times more than Hooke's instrument.

questions.question: Which comparison of magnifications given in the chapter is correct?
options: A paper microscope shows more detail than a lab microscope
Hooke's microscope was weaker than any microscope used today
An electron microscope magnifies a cell only about 1,000 times
Hooke's 200–300× lies inside the 100–400× range used for microbes
questions.explanation: Microbes are viewed with microscopes of 100–400×, and Hooke's 200–300× falls inside that range. Electron microscopes reach about 10,00,000×, and paper microscopes give less detail than lab ones.

questions.question: Select ALL the things the chapter credits to Antonie van Leeuwenhoek.
questions.explanation: Leeuwenhoek made better lenses, built more useful microscopes and first described bacteria and blood cells. Micrographia, the word 'cell' and the cork drawings belong to Hooke.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: Which stain is used on the onion peel in Activity 2.2?
questions.explanation: Safranin is a red stain that gives the onion cells a pinkish colour. Methylene blue is used for cheek cells; glycerin is not a stain.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: Which stain is added to the cheek-cell scraping in Activity 2.3?
questions.explanation: Methylene blue, a blue stain, is added to the cheek cells to increase contrast. Safranin is the red stain used for onion peel.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: What is the purpose of putting a drop of glycerin on the mounted peel or cheek cells?
options: It stops the cells drying and improves clarity
It colours the cells so they show up clearly
It kills any microbes present on the slide
It glues the coverslip firmly to the slide
questions.explanation: Glycerin prevents the cells from drying out and improves clarity for better viewing. Colouring is the job of the stain, not glycerin.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: Why is a stain added before observing cells under the microscope?
options: It increases contrast so the cells are more visible
It makes the cells grow larger on the slide
It stops air bubbles forming under the coverslip
It preserves the cells for several weeks
questions.explanation: Adding a stain increases contrast between the cell parts and the background, improving visibility under the microscope.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: The coverslip is lowered slowly with a needle, at an angle. What does this prevent?
questions.explanation: Lowering the coverslip slowly at an angle keeps air bubbles from being trapped, which would spoil the view of the cells.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: In both cell-mounting activities, blotting paper is used to
options: spread the cells evenly on the slide
dry the cells before staining them
wipe extra glycerin from the coverslip edges
press the coverslip flat onto the peel
questions.explanation: Blotting paper gently soaks up the extra glycerin around the edges of the coverslip.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: Under a microscope a student sees polygon-shaped cells with a nucleus but no cell wall, spread loosely on the slide. These are most likely
questions.explanation: Cheek cells are polygon-shaped and, being animal cells, have no cell wall. Onion peel cells are nearly rectangular, tightly packed and have a cell wall.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: Which difference would a student actually observe between onion peel cells and cheek cells?
options: Cheek cells have a nucleus; onion cells do not
Onion cells have a cell wall; cheek cells do not
Onion cells have no cytoplasm; cheek cells do
Cheek cells are rectangular; onion cells polygonal
questions.explanation: Both kinds of cells have a nucleus and cytoplasm. The key difference is the extra outer cell wall in onion (plant) cells; the shapes are the other way round — onion rectangular, cheek polygonal.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: Safranin gives onion peel cells a pinkish colour so that they can be seen clearly.
questions.explanation: The chapter says safranin, a red stain, gives the cells a pinkish colour and helps us see them clearly.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: In Activity 2.2, methylene blue is used to stain the onion peel cells.
questions.explanation: The onion peel is stained with safranin (red). Methylene blue is the stain used for human cheek cells in Activity 2.3.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: The cheek cells scraped in Activity 2.3 come from the
questions.explanation: The blunt end of a toothpick gently scrapes the inside of the cheek; these cells form the inner lining of the mouth.

questions.topic: Observing Cells: Onion Peel and Cheek Cells
questions.question: Select ALL the steps that are common to BOTH the onion peel activity (2.2) and the cheek cell activity (2.3).
questions.explanation: Both activities stain the material, add glycerin and place a coverslip. Safranin and forceps are specific to the onion peel; cheek cells use methylene blue and a toothpick.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three basic parts of every cell?
questions.explanation: The three basic parts are the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. A cell wall is an extra layer found only in some cells, such as plant cells.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: What is the main job of the cell membrane?
options: To separate cells and control what enters and leaves
To make food for the cell using sunlight energy
To regulate every activity and the growth of the cell
To give the cell rigidity, strength and a firm shape
questions.explanation: The cell membrane encloses the cytoplasm and nucleus, separates cells, and is porous so useful materials enter and waste leaves. Regulation is the nucleus; rigidity is the cell wall.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: Which part of the cell regulates all activities within the cell and also regulates growth?
questions.explanation: The nucleus regulates all the cell's activities and its growth. Most life processes happen in the cytoplasm, but it is the nucleus that regulates them.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: Where do most of the life processes of a cell take place?
questions.explanation: Most life processes occur in the cytoplasm, which contains compounds such as carbohydrates, proteins, fats and mineral salts.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: The cell membrane is described as 'porous'. What does this allow?
options: Movement of the nucleus inside the cell
Entry of essential materials and exit of waste
Light to pass in for photosynthesis
The cell to stay rigid and firm
questions.explanation: Being porous, the membrane lets materials needed for life processes enter and waste materials leave the cell.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: The nucleus is itself covered by
questions.explanation: The chapter says the nucleus, the round structure in the middle, is also covered by a thin membrane.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: The nucleus is the outermost layer of a cell.
questions.explanation: The outermost layer of an animal cell is the cell membrane (plant cells have a cell wall outside that). The nucleus is the round structure in the middle.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: According to the chapter, which of these compounds does the cytoplasm contain? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The cytoplasm contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats and mineral salts. Chlorophyll is in plastids (chloroplasts), and lactic acid is a product of Lactobacillus, not a cell component.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: If the nucleus of a cell were damaged, which of the following would be MOST directly affected?
options: Regulation of the cell's activities and growth
The entry of water through the porous membrane
The colour of the cell seen under the microscope
The thickness and rigidity of the cell wall
questions.explanation: The nucleus regulates all activities and growth, so damage to it directly affects regulation. Entry of water is a membrane job; colour comes from stains or chlorophyll.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: Which structure gives plant cells rigidity and makes them look firm and compactly arranged?
questions.explanation: The cell wall provides rigidity and strength, which is why plant cells are arranged compactly and look firm.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: The space between the cell membrane and the nucleus is filled with cytoplasm.
questions.explanation: The chapter defines cytoplasm as the material filling the space between the cell membrane and the nucleus.

questions.topic: Parts of a Cell and Their Functions
questions.question: A student says: 'The nucleus does most of the cell's life processes, so it is the most active part.' Which correction is right?
options: The nucleus does nothing; only the membrane is active
Most life processes occur in the cell wall, not the nucleus
Most life processes occur in the cytoplasm; the nucleus regulates them
The nucleus carries out the life processes and also stores food
questions.explanation: The chapter places most life processes in the cytoplasm, while the nucleus regulates the cell's activities and growth. The two roles are different.

questions.question: Which extra outer layer do onion peel cells have that cheek cells lack?
questions.explanation: Plant cells such as onion peel cells have a cell wall outside the cell membrane; animal cells like cheek cells do not.

questions.question: What are plastids?
options: Large empty-looking spaces that store waste in plant cells
Tiny rod-shaped structures found in cells of all parts of a plant
Thin branched filaments that lack any chlorophyll
Round structures in the middle of a cell that regulate growth
questions.explanation: Plastids are tiny rod-shaped structures in plant cells. Some (chloroplasts) hold chlorophyll; in non-green parts they store substances. The vacuole is the empty-looking space.

questions.question: In the non-green parts of a plant, what do plastids mainly do?
questions.explanation: Only green plastids (chloroplasts) do photosynthesis. In non-green parts plastids help in storage of substances.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a role of the large vacuole in a plant cell, according to the chapter?
options: Maintaining the shape of the cell
questions.explanation: The vacuole stores substances, removes waste and maintains cell shape, giving strength and support. Food-making (photosynthesis) is done by chloroplasts.

questions.question: Which statement about vacuoles is NOT correct?
options: Animal cells always have one large central vacuole
Plant-cell vacuoles help maintain the shape of the cell
Vacuoles in animal cells, when present, are usually small
Small vacuoles store substances dissolved in water
questions.explanation: In animal cells vacuoles are usually absent, and when present they are small. It is the plant cell that has a large vacuole.

questions.question: Based on Fig. 2.5, select ALL the parts found in a plant cell but NOT in an animal cell.
questions.explanation: Cell wall and chloroplasts (and a large vacuole) are plant-cell features. Nucleus, cell membrane and cytoplasm are present in both cell types.

questions.question: Chloroplasts are green because they contain chlorophyll.
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are plastids that contain chlorophyll, which makes them green and lets them carry out photosynthesis.

questions.question: A cell is just a simple bag of liquid.
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that a cell is a complex structure made of many parts, each with its own special function.

questions.question: A cell seen under a microscope is green, has a rigid outer covering and one big central space. It is most likely
questions.explanation: Green colour (chloroplasts), a rigid wall and a large vacuole are the hallmarks of a plant cell. Animal cells lack all three, and bacteria have no large vacuole or chloroplasts.

questions.question: Which of these is common to BOTH plant and animal cells?
questions.explanation: Both cell types have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. Cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole are plant-only.

questions.question: In which part of a plant are plastids most likely to contain chlorophyll?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll-containing plastids (chloroplasts) make parts green; leaves are green. In non-green parts such as roots, plastids store substances instead.

questions.question: What is the shape of a human muscle cell?
questions.explanation: Muscle cells are spindle-shaped. Nerve cells are long and branched, cheek cells polygonal and onion cells rectangular.

questions.question: Which description fits a nerve cell (neuron)?
questions.explanation: A nerve cell is very long and has branches, which help it reach different body parts and pass on messages.

questions.question: Why does the long, branched shape of a neuron suit its job?
options: It lets the cell store large amounts of food
It helps it reach distant parts and pass messages quickly
It allows the cell to contract and relax in waves
It protects the inner surface of the cheek
questions.explanation: Neurons carry messages; their elongated, branched structure helps them reach different parts of the body and transmit messages fast.

questions.question: Inner cheek cells are thin and flat. What function does this shape serve?
options: Pushing food down the food pipe
questions.explanation: Thin, flat cheek cells form a protective lining on the inner surface of the cheek.

questions.question: Muscle cells in the food pipe push food to the stomach. Which property makes this wave-like movement possible?
options: They are round and filled with vacuoles
They are long, branched and rigid
They are rectangular with a cell wall
They are thin, flexible and spindle-shaped
questions.explanation: The muscle cells contract and relax in waves; this works because they are thin, flexible and spindle-shaped.

questions.question: Which statement about cells of the stomach is NOT correct?
options: Muscle cells in the stomach wall help churn the food
Muscle cells of the stomach produce the digestive acid
Cells in the inner lining produce digestive juices and acid
Different types of cells work together to make digestion possible
questions.explanation: Acid and digestive juices come from other cells in the stomach's inner lining, not from the muscle cells, whose job is churning.

questions.question: Nerve cells are also known as neurons.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that nerve cells, also known as neurons, carry messages in our body.

questions.question: All cells in the human body have the same shape and differ only in size.
questions.explanation: Human cells vary in shape — muscle cells are spindle-shaped, nerve cells long and branched, cheek cells flat and polygonal — because shape is related to function.

questions.question: Select ALL the shapes the chapter mentions for plant cells.
questions.explanation: Plant cells may be rectangular, elongated, oval or tube-like. Spindle is a muscle-cell shape, spiral is a bacterial shape and branched describes nerve cells or fungal filaments.

questions.question: The chapter says the unique shape, size and structure of a cell are related to its
questions.explanation: Cells look different because their shape and structure help them carry out their specific functions.

questions.question: A newly discovered cell must carry signals quickly across a long distance in the body. Which shape would you expect it to have?
questions.explanation: Carrying messages across distances is the role of neurons, whose long, branched shape suits exactly this task.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the levels of organisation in a living organism?
options: Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism
Tissue → Cell → Organ → Organism → Organ system
Cell → Organ → Tissue → Organ system → Organism
Organ → Tissue → Cell → Organ system → Organism
questions.explanation: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems, and all organ systems together make up the organism.

questions.question: A group of similar cells performing a function is called
questions.explanation: A tissue is a group of similar cells. Different tissues organise to form an organ.

questions.question: Different tissues organised together form
questions.explanation: An organ is made of different tissues organised together; several organs make an organ system.

questions.question: The stomach contains muscle tissue and lining tissue that produces acid. In the levels of organisation, the stomach is
questions.explanation: Because the stomach is made of different tissues working together, it is an organ. The whole digestive system, with many organs, is the organ system.

questions.question: A tissue is the basic unit of life.
questions.explanation: The cell is the basic unit of life, like a brick in a wall. A tissue is a group of similar cells.

questions.question: According to the chapter, the life of a complex multicellular organism begins with
options: a single cell called the egg
questions.explanation: Life begins with a single cell — the egg — which divides repeatedly to form a complete many-celled organism.

questions.question: Organisms made up of many cells are called
questions.explanation: Multicellular means many-celled. Animals, including humans, and plants are multicellular.

questions.question: Plants are multicellular organisms but animals are not.
questions.explanation: Both plants and animals (including humans) are multicellular; they develop from a single egg cell dividing repeatedly.

questions.question: What is the largest known cell in the living world?
options: The yolk of an ostrich egg
The white of a hen's egg
questions.explanation: The yolk of an ostrich egg is a single cell, about 130–170 mm across — the largest known cell. The egg white is non-cellular material.

questions.question: Apart from the yolk cell, an ostrich egg contains non-cellular material. What is it for?
options: A layer of chlorophyll to make food for the embryo
A second cell that divides to form the chick
A shell for protection and a white liquid that nourishes the cell
Bacteria that help the yolk digest nutrients
questions.explanation: The shell protects, and the white liquid nourishes the developing cell. Neither is a cell.

questions.question: The ostrich yolk cell measures about 130–170 mm in diameter. In centimetres this is about
questions.explanation: 10 mm = 1 cm, so 130–170 mm = 13–17 cm — roughly the width of a notebook, a huge size for a single cell.

questions.question: The egg of an organism can divide repeatedly to form a complete living being made of many cells.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the egg has the amazing ability to divide repeatedly, forming a multicellular organism.

questions.question: Select ALL the organisms that are multicellular.
questions.explanation: Humans, plants and mould (a multicellular fungus) are many-celled. Amoeba and bacteria are single-celled.

questions.question: The chapter compares a cell to a brick. Which pairing completes the analogy correctly?
options: Cell is to brick as tissue is to wall
Cell is to organism as brick is to wall
Cell is to wall as brick is to organism
Brick is to cell as organism is to tissue
questions.explanation: A cell is the basic unit of a living organism in the same way that a brick is the basic unit of a wall.

questions.question: What are microorganisms?
options: Plants and animals that are smaller than an ant
Non-living particles floating in pond water
Any organism that lives inside the human body
Living beings too small to be seen with the naked eye
questions.explanation: 'Micro' means very small; microorganisms are tiny living beings that cannot be seen without a microscope.

questions.question: In the word 'microorganism', 'micro' means
questions.explanation: Micro means very small and organism means living being — a very small living being.

questions.question: Which pair of microorganisms is given in the chapter as unicellular?
questions.explanation: Bacteria and Amoeba are made of just one cell. Some fungi (mould) and algae are multicellular.

questions.question: In Table 2.1 (pond water), which organism was recorded as a single cell with an irregular shape that moves?
questions.explanation: Amoeba was recorded as 'single cell, moving, irregular shape'. Paramecium moves using specialised structures; algae are green.

questions.question: In Table 2.2, a 'branched filament without chlorophyll having a brush-like structure' describes
questions.explanation: Mould was recorded as a brush-like branched filament; bread mould had a sac-like structure. Both lack chlorophyll.

questions.question: A soil-suspension organism is a branched filament without chlorophyll and has a sac-like structure. According to Table 2.2 it is
questions.explanation: Bread mould is the sac-like branched filament; the brush-like one is the other mould. Algae are spherical and have chlorophyll.

questions.question: Select ALL the shapes of bacteria listed in Table 2.2.
questions.explanation: Bacteria were recorded as spherical, comma, spiral or rod-shaped. Branched filaments are fungi; spindle shape is a muscle cell.

questions.question: The microscopes used to see the organisms in Tables 2.1 and 2.2 magnify about
questions.explanation: The chapter says we can only see these microorganisms with a microscope that magnifies them 100 to 400 times.

questions.question: Which statement about viruses is correct?
options: They are acellular and multiply only inside a living cell
They are single-celled and move with hair-like structures
They are multicellular and can infect only plants
They have a nucleoid like bacteria and live in soil
questions.explanation: Viruses are microscopic and acellular (not made of cells). They multiply only when they enter a living cell, and can infect plants, animals or bacteria.

questions.question: Viruses can infect bacterial cells.
questions.explanation: The chapter says viruses may infect plants, animals or bacterial cells and may cause disease.

questions.question: Viruses are unicellular microorganisms.
questions.explanation: Viruses are acellular — they are not made of cells at all, which is why they reproduce only inside a host cell.

questions.question: Which statement about microorganisms is NOT correct?
options: Some microorganisms live inside our bodies
All microorganisms are made of a single cell
Microorganisms are found in water, soil and air
Some fungi and algae are multicellular microbes
questions.explanation: Not all microbes are unicellular: some fungi (mould) and algae have many cells. The other three statements are from the chapter.

questions.question: What is the advantage of a low-cost foldable paper microscope mentioned in the chapter?
options: It can show subcellular parts like an electron microscope
It gives more detail than a high-powered lab microscope
It makes the microscopic world accessible to many people
It works without any lens at all
questions.explanation: The paper microscope may give less detail than lab microscopes, but being low-cost and foldable it makes microscopy accessible to many.

questions.question: In Activity 2.5, after stirring soil in water and letting it settle, from where is the drop for the slide taken?
options: From the mud at the bottom
From the top layer of the liquid
questions.explanation: The suspension is left to settle and a drop is taken from the top layer, so the slide is not clouded by heavy soil particles.

questions.question: Both pond water (Activity 2.4) and soil suspension (Activity 2.5) showed small moving organisms. What does this indicate?
options: Pond water had been mixed into the soil beforehand
Microorganisms are present in soil as well as in water
Only wet places can contain any microorganisms
Soil organisms are the same species as pond ones
questions.explanation: Seeing similar tiny creatures in both samples shows that soil, like water, contains a variety of microorganisms invisible to the unaided eye.

questions.question: Amoeba and Paramecium both belong to which group of microorganisms?
questions.explanation: Table 2.1 labels both Amoeba and Paramecium as Protozoa.

questions.question: A lemon left outside develops a powdery, cotton-like growth after some days. What has happened?
options: Its sugar has turned into salt
It has been infected by microbes
questions.explanation: The powdery or cotton-like growth on rotting food is microbes (such as mould) that have infected it.

questions.question: Which pair of EXTREME conditions does the chapter say some microbes can live in?
options: Hot water springs and snow-cold zones
Deep space and the surface of the Sun
Boiling oil and hot desert sand dunes
Pure salt crystals and pure sugar
questions.explanation: Some microbes live in extreme climates such as hot water springs and snow-cold zones, as well as at moderate temperatures.

questions.question: Why do microorganisms not spoil pickles and murabbas?
options: Oil makes the microbes unable to see food
The spices kill every microbe present
Pickles are kept sealed away from all air
High salt or sugar concentration stops them growing
questions.explanation: Pickles and murabbas contain spices with a high concentration of salt or sugar, which act as preservatives and do not allow microbes to grow.

questions.question: Microorganisms cannot survive in hot water springs.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives hot water springs as an example of an extreme condition where some microorganisms do live.

questions.question: Which of these foods is LEAST likely to be spoiled by microbes?
options: A lemon left outside for a week
A cut tomato left on the table
A jar of murabba in thick sugar syrup
questions.explanation: High sugar concentration in murabba prevents microbial growth. The other foods are moist and unpreserved, so microbes grow on them.

questions.question: Pickles are preserved mainly because the spices kill the microbes.
questions.explanation: The chapter attributes preservation to the high concentration of salt or sugar, which does not allow microbes to grow — not to spices killing them.

questions.question: Which set lists the three microbe shapes mentioned when discussing Tables 2.1 and 2.2 on page 11?
questions.explanation: Microorganisms vary in shape — spherical, rod-shaped or irregular, as seen in the tables. The other sets describe plant or animal cells.

questions.question: Some microorganisms live inside the human intestine and help in digestion.
questions.explanation: The chapter recalls that our intestine has many bacteria that help in digestion.

questions.question: Which of these are given in the chapter as EXTREME conditions where microbes live? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Hot springs and snow-cold zones are the extreme examples. Moderate temperature is not extreme, and high sugar stops microbes growing.

questions.question: Like plants and animals, microorganisms show great diversity. Which statement does NOT follow from the chapter?
options: All microbes need moderate temperatures to survive
Microbes vary in shape, size and structure
Microbes live in water, soil, air and inside bodies
Microbes can be found on leaves, stems and roots
questions.explanation: Some microbes live in extreme hot or cold places, so 'all need moderate temperatures' is wrong. The other three are stated in the chapter.

questions.question: In Activity 2.7, what do fruit and vegetable peels buried in soil turn into after 2–3 weeks?
options: A green layer of pond algae
questions.explanation: The peels become a dark-coloured material — manure — that is rich in nutrients and increases soil fertility.

questions.question: Which microorganisms break down plant waste into manure?
questions.explanation: Fungi and bacteria in soil act on plant waste and slowly break it down into simpler, nutrient-rich manure.

questions.question: What does the chapter call the process by which microbes break down complex substances of fallen leaves into simpler nutrient-rich substances?
questions.explanation: This breakdown of complex substances into simpler ones that return to the soil is decomposition.

questions.question: According to the chapter, manure formation occurs best at
options: any temperature as long as there is no water
questions.explanation: Manure formation occurs at optimal temperature and appropriate moisture level — the conditions microbes need to grow.

questions.question: Suppose microorganisms suddenly vanished from Earth. Which consequence follows from the chapter?
options: Plants would grow faster since nothing would attack their roots
Dead matter would not decompose and soil would lose nutrients
All food would stay fresh forever and soil would get richer
Curd and bread could still be made but would taste the same
questions.explanation: Microbes decompose dead matter and recycle nutrients to the soil; without them waste would pile up and soil would lose fertility. Curd and bread also depend on microbes.

questions.question: In what kind of environment do the microbes that produce biogas live?
questions.explanation: Many bacteria and fungi live in an oxygen-free environment; some of these decompose waste and release biogas.

questions.question: Biogas is mainly made of two gases. Which is present in the HIGHER proportion?
questions.explanation: Biogas is primarily carbon dioxide plus a high proportion of methane; methane is the main gas and the fuel component.

questions.question: Select ALL the uses of biogas mentioned in the chapter.
questions.explanation: Biogas is used for cooking, heating, generating electricity and even running vehicles. Pickles are preserved by salt or sugar, not gas.

questions.question: What did Ananda Mohan Chakrabarty develop in 1971?
options: A bacterium that could break down oil spills
A yeast strain that makes bread rise much faster
A chemical fertiliser that is rich in nitrogen
questions.explanation: Chakrabarty developed a special bacterium that could break down oil spills, helping to clean the environment.

questions.question: What is a patent, as described in the chapter?
options: A book that publishes drawings of new discoveries
A prize given to a scientist for a famous discovery
A licence allowing anyone to use a new invention freely
A right so no one can copy, use or sell an invention without permission
questions.explanation: A patent is a copyright given so that no one else can copy, use or sell the invention without the inventor's permission.

questions.question: Chakrabarty developed his bacterium in 1971 and received a patent in 1980. How many years passed between the two?
In the Vedas, the word 'Krimi' refers to
options: the fermentation of milk into sour curd
tiny entities, both visible and invisible
the very large yolk cell of an ostrich egg
the lentil-shaped lens of early microscopes
questions.explanation: Ancient texts use 'Krimi' for tiny entities including Drishya (visible) and Adrishya (invisible), with mention of their beneficial and harmful effects.

questions.question: Biogas is mostly carbon dioxide with only a small amount of methane.
questions.explanation: Biogas contains carbon dioxide but a HIGH proportion of methane — methane is the main component.

questions.question: Exercise 4: Snehal put peels mixed with dried leaves in pit A and the same peels without leaves in pit B, covered both and waited 3 weeks. What is she testing?
options: Whether dried leaves affect how waste turns into manure
Whether fruit peels can sprout into new plants in soil
Whether sunlight is needed for the waste to decompose
Whether the garden soil contains Rhizobium bacteria
questions.explanation: The only difference between the pits is the dried leaves, so she is testing their effect on decomposition/manure formation. Both pits are covered, so sunlight is not the variable.

questions.question: Helpful bacteria can also decompose animal wastes such as dung.
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that helpful bacteria decompose animal wastes like dung as well as plant waste.

questions.question: Exercise 6 asks you to test that microbes need certain conditions for growth. Which of these is NOT one of the conditions named?
questions.explanation: The exercise names optimal temperature, air and moisture. Sunlight is not listed — indeed Activity 2.7 works with the waste buried under soil.

questions.question: Exercise 7: one bread slice is kept near the sink, the other in the refrigerator for three days. Why does the fridge slice show little or no mould?
options: The fridge has no air for microbes
The cold slows the growth of microbes
Light in the fridge kills the microbes
Bread in the cold turns into manure
questions.explanation: Microbes grow well in warm, moist conditions; the low temperature of the refrigerator slows their growth, while the damp warm sink area favours mould.

questions.question: Yeast belongs to which group of microorganisms?
questions.explanation: Yeast is a unicellular fungus.

questions.question: Why does dough with yeast rise and become fluffy?
options: Yeast produces lactic acid that puffs the dough
Yeast absorbs water and swells inside the dough
Sugar reacts with warm air and expands the flour
Yeast respires and releases carbon dioxide that forms bubbles
questions.explanation: Yeast breaks down food during respiration and releases carbon dioxide; the gas bubbles make the dough soft and fluffy.

questions.question: The dough with yeast develops a slightly different smell. This is because yeast also produces
questions.explanation: Yeast produces a small amount of alcohol during respiration, which gives the dough its characteristic smell.

questions.question: Why are sugar and warm water added to the flour in Activity 2.8?
options: Sugar makes bubbles and warm water traps them
Sugar sweetens the bread and warm water melts the flour
Sugar kills unwanted bacteria and warm water sterilises
Sugar is food for the yeast and warmth helps it grow
questions.explanation: Yeast respires by breaking down food (sugar) and grows well in warm conditions, so both help it work faster.

questions.question: In Activity 2.8, why was NO yeast added to bowl B?
options: To make bowl B rise faster than A
Because bowl B already had enough sugar
So that the two bowls could be compared
Because yeast only works in bowl A's flour
questions.explanation: Bowl B is the control — identical except for yeast — so any difference in the dough can be attributed to the yeast.

questions.question: Which bacterium does the chapter name for fermenting idli and dosa batter and bhatura dough?
questions.explanation: Besides yeast, some bacteria such as Lactobacillus help ferment batter for idli and dosa and dough for bhatura.

questions.question: Yeast is a unicellular fungus.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that yeast is a unicellular fungus while mould is a multicellular fungus.

questions.question: Yeast produces lactic acid, which makes the dough soft and fluffy.
questions.explanation: Yeast releases carbon dioxide (and a little alcohol). Lactic acid is produced by Lactobacillus in curd.

questions.question: Exercise 2(i): Both test tubes had sugar solution; only tube B had yeast. After 3–4 hours in a warm place the balloon on B inflated. Why?
options: Sugar reacted with warm air to form gas
Water evaporated and filled the balloon
Warm air expanded inside tube B only
Yeast produced a gas inside tube B
questions.explanation: Only tube B differed by having yeast, and warm air or evaporation would affect both tubes equally. The yeast respired on the sugar and released carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Exercise 2(ii): Aanandi shook the gas from the balloon into lime water. What was she trying to find out?
options: Whether the gas was carbon dioxide
Whether sugar remained in the tube
questions.explanation: Lime water is a test for carbon dioxide (it turns milky), so she wanted to confirm the gas produced by yeast was carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Exercise 9(iii): If yeast were NOT added to flask A containing warm sugar solution, what would be observed in the lime water in tube B?
options: It would turn milky faster than before
No change, because no gas would be produced
It would turn green from algae
It would boil due to the warm solution
questions.explanation: Without yeast there is no respiration and no carbon dioxide, so the lime water stays clear.

questions.question: Which statement about yeast is NOT correct?
options: It produces lactic acid that sours dough
It belongs to the group of organisms called fungi
It grows well in warm conditions
It releases carbon dioxide while respiring
questions.explanation: Yeast releases carbon dioxide and a little alcohol — not lactic acid, which is a Lactobacillus product. The other three are correct.

questions.question: Select ALL the foods the chapter says are made using yeast.
questions.explanation: Yeasts are used for breads, cakes and pastries. Curd is made by Lactobacillus and manure by decomposer microbes.

questions.question: In Exercise 2, why was the set-up kept in a warm place away from sunlight?
options: Yeast grows well in warm conditions
Cold makes balloons expand on their own
Warmth melts the sugar into gas
questions.explanation: Yeast is a fungus that grows well in warmth; it has no chlorophyll, so sunlight is irrelevant to its food-making.

questions.question: Which bacterium in curd ferments milk into curd?
questions.explanation: Curd contains several bacteria; one of them, Lactobacillus, feeds on the milk sugar and ferments it into curd.

questions.question: What does Lactobacillus feed on in milk?
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus feeds on lactose (milk sugar), multiplies and ferments the milk.

questions.question: Why does curd taste sour?
options: Salt is added as a preservative
questions.explanation: Instead of alcohol (like yeast), these bacteria produce lactic acid, which makes curd sour.

questions.question: In Activity 2.9, milk in bowl A (warm) curdled but milk in bowl B (cold) did not. Why?
options: Cold milk has no lactose for the bacteria to eat
The curd bacteria grow well in warm conditions
Warm milk contains more fat than cold milk
Bowl B was not covered as well as bowl A was
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus grows well in warm conditions, so curd formed in the warm bowl but not in the cold one.

questions.question: Exercise 8: Curd left out for a day becomes more sour. Which explanation fits the chapter?
options: Water evaporates leaving the sugar concentrated
The curd absorbs sour gases from the air around it
Yeast from the air adds alcohol to the curd
Bacteria keep multiplying and making more lactic acid
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus continues to feed on lactose and multiply at room temperature, producing more lactic acid and increasing sourness.

questions.question: Yeast and Lactobacillus both ferment food. What is the key difference in their products?
options: Yeast gives methane; Lactobacillus gives oxygen
Yeast gives lactic acid; Lactobacillus gives alcohol
Yeast gives alcohol; Lactobacillus gives lactic acid
Both give alcohol but in different amounts
questions.explanation: Yeast produces carbon dioxide and a little alcohol; Lactobacillus produces lactic acid instead of alcohol.

questions.question: Lactobacillus feeds on lactose, the sugar in milk.
questions.explanation: The chapter says this bacterium feeds on the sugar in the milk (lactose), multiplies and ferments it.

questions.question: In bowl B (cold), the milk did not curdle but might be slightly sour. How can both observations be explained?
options: Cold slows the bacteria, so only a little lactic acid forms
Cold milk has twice as much lactose as warm milk
The bacteria die instantly in cold, leaving sour gas
Sourness comes from yeast, curdling from bacteria
questions.explanation: The bacteria grow poorly in the cold, so a small amount of acid may form (slight sourness) but not enough to curdle the milk.

questions.question: Select ALL the statements that are true of Lactobacillus.
options: It ferments idli and dosa batter
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus is a bacterium used for curd and fermenting batter. It produces lactic acid, not alcohol, and being a cell it is not acellular (that describes viruses).

questions.question: Curd becomes sour because of alcohol produced by bacteria.
questions.explanation: The sourness comes from lactic acid produced by Lactobacillus. Alcohol is produced by yeast, not by these bacteria.

questions.question: Apart from home curd-making, where else does the chapter say Lactobacillus is used?
options: Cleaning up oil spills at sea
questions.explanation: The Snapshots note that Lactobacillus is used in curd formation at home and in fermentation processes in the food industry.

questions.question: Where does the bacterium Rhizobium live?
options: In the leaves of wheat plants
questions.explanation: Rhizobium lives in swollen regions called nodules on the roots of legumes such as beans, peas and lentils.

questions.question: What does Rhizobium do for the plant it lives with?
options: Produces lactic acid that protects the roots
Traps nitrogen from the air for the plant to use
Releases oxygen for the roots to breathe with
Breaks the dead roots down into rich manure
questions.explanation: Rhizobium traps nitrogen from the air and converts it into a form plants can use, helping them grow without chemical fertiliser.

questions.question: Which group of crops have root nodules containing Rhizobium?
options: Legumes such as beans, peas and lentils
Cereals such as wheat and rice
Vegetables such as tomato and onion
Fruits such as lemon and orange
questions.explanation: Roots of certain legumes — beans, peas, lentils (and cowpea in Fig. 2.12) — have nodules with Rhizobium.

questions.question: Exercise 3: A wheat farmer added nitrogen fertiliser but a neighbour growing beans did not. Why could the bean farmer skip it?
options: Rhizobium in bean root nodules supplies nitrogen naturally
Beans do not need any nitrogen to grow at all
Bean plants take nitrogen directly from rain water
Beans grow better in soil that is poor in nutrients
questions.explanation: Beans are legumes; Rhizobium in their root nodules traps nitrogen from the air, so extra nitrogen fertiliser is not needed. Wheat has no such nodules.

questions.question: Why do farmers grow legumes in rotation with other crops?
options: Legumes kill harmful microbes in the soil
Legumes naturally raise soil nitrogen for the next crop
Legumes need less water than any other crop
Legumes shade the soil and keep it cool
questions.explanation: Rhizobium in legume roots adds nitrogen to the soil, keeping it healthy for the following crop without chemical fertiliser.

questions.question: Rhizobium lives in nodules found on the leaves of legume plants.
questions.explanation: The nodules are swollen regions on the ROOTS of legumes, not the leaves.

questions.question: Growing legumes in rotation with other crops helps keep the soil healthy for the next crop.
questions.explanation: Legumes naturally increase nitrogen in the soil, so rotation keeps it fertile.

questions.question: Exercise 5 riddle: 'I live in the roots of pulse crops and provide nutrients for their growth.' Who am I?
questions.explanation: Pulses are legumes; the microbe in their root nodules that provides nitrogen nutrients is Rhizobium.

questions.question: What are root nodules?
options: Green parts of roots with chlorophyll
Tiny hairs that absorb water from soil
Dark patches of decaying root tissue
Swollen regions on roots where Rhizobium lives
questions.explanation: Nodules are swollen regions on the roots of legumes in which Rhizobium bacteria live.

questions.question: Select ALL the plants that the chapter says have root nodules with Rhizobium.
questions.explanation: Beans and peas (and lentils) are legumes with Rhizobium nodules. Wheat, rice and maize are cereals without them — which is why the wheat farmer in Exercise 3 needs fertiliser.

questions.question: Which statement about Rhizobium and legumes is NOT correct?
options: Rhizobium traps nitrogen from the air
Rhizobium makes the plant's leaves produce chlorophyll
Legumes can grow well without chemical nitrogen fertiliser
Fig. 2.12 shows nodules on a cowpea plant
questions.explanation: Rhizobium's contribution is nitrogen, not chlorophyll. The other three statements are from the chapter.

questions.question: How do microalgae make their food?
questions.explanation: Microalgae are plant-like; they make their own food using sunlight and release oxygen while doing so.

questions.question: What share of Earth's oxygen supply do microalgae produce, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: While making food, microalgae release oxygen and produce more than half of Earth's oxygen supply.

questions.question: Which three microalgae does the chapter name as human health supplements and medicines?
questions.explanation: Spirulina, Chlorella and Diatoms are used by humans as health supplements and medicines.

questions.question: Besides food and oxygen, which two uses of microalgae does the chapter give?
options: Breaking down oil spills and dung
questions.explanation: Microalgae help clean water and are used to make biofuel.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as a threat to microalgal diversity?
questions.explanation: Pollution, climate change and habitat destruction threaten microalgae. Farming Spirulina is given as a livelihood and conservation-friendly practice.

questions.question: Spirulina is called a 'superfood'. Which fact from the chapter supports this?
options: It is made up mostly of fat and sugar
Over 60 per cent of its body weight is protein
It contains chlorophyll just like a green leaf
It can be harvested from the tank every day
questions.explanation: Spirulina is rich in protein (over 60% of body weight), a good source of vitamin B12, and has only a small amount of fat and sugar.

questions.question: Which statement about growing Spirulina is NOT correct?
options: The tank should be kept in direct sunlight
The tank is filled with pond water
It is stirred twice a week
It is harvested after 3–6 weeks by filtering through a fine cloth
questions.explanation: The tank is placed in a bright place but AWAY from direct sunlight, under a shade net or at moderate temperature.

questions.question: Spirulina is a bacterium that traps nitrogen in root nodules.
questions.explanation: Spirulina is a microalga used as a superfood. Nitrogen-trapping in root nodules is done by the bacterium Rhizobium.

questions.question: Microalgae serve as a food source for many aquatic animals.
questions.explanation: The chapter says microalgae are rich in nutrients and serve as food for many aquatic animals.

questions.question: Select ALL the microalgae named in the chapter.
questions.explanation: Spirulina and Chlorella (and Diatoms) are microalgae. Rhizobium and Lactobacillus are bacteria; Amoeba is a protozoan.

questions.question: Spirulina is stirred twice a week and harvested after 3–6 weeks. How many times would it be stirred in total before harvest?
questions.explanation: Twice a week for 3 weeks is 6 stirs; for 6 weeks it is 12 stirs — so 6 to 12 times.

questions.question: Spirulina contains a large amount of fat and sugar.
questions.explanation: Spirulina has only a SMALL amount of fat and sugar; it is rich in protein.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Instead of a well-defined nucleus, a bacterial cell has a
questions.explanation: Bacteria lack a well-defined nucleus and a nuclear membrane; they have a nucleoid region instead (Fig. 2.13).

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Fungal cells have a cell wall but cannot photosynthesise. Why?
questions.explanation: Fungi have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, so they cannot make their own food through photosynthesis.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: According to the Snapshots, which cells have a cell wall around the cell membrane?
questions.explanation: Plant, fungal and bacterial cells have an extra covering, the cell wall. Animal cells do not.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: To observe subcellular components, the chapter says we need
questions.explanation: Subcellular structures need very high magnification; an electron microscope magnifies about 10,00,000 times.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Which of these cells lacks a nuclear membrane?
questions.explanation: Bacteria have no well-defined nucleus or nuclear membrane. Yeast, protozoa (Amoeba), algae, plants and animals all have a proper nucleus.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Select ALL the organisms that are unicellular.
questions.explanation: Bacteria and protozoa are single-celled (so is yeast). Mould is a multicellular fungus, and plants and humans are multicellular.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Yeast is unicellular and mould is multicellular, yet both are placed in the same group. Which group?
questions.explanation: Fungi can be unicellular (yeast) or multicellular (mould); both lack chloroplasts and have a cell wall.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Which statement is NOT correct?
options: All microorganisms lack a well-defined nucleus
Fungi cannot make their own food
Viruses reproduce only inside a host
questions.explanation: Only bacteria lack a well-defined nucleus; yeast, protozoa and algae have one. The other statements are correct.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Protozoa have a well-defined nucleus, unlike bacteria.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the nucleoid distinguishes bacteria from the cells of yeast, protozoa, algae, fungi, plants and animals, which have a nucleus.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Fungi can make their own food because their cells have a cell wall.
questions.explanation: Food-making needs chloroplasts, not a cell wall. Fungi have a cell wall but no chloroplasts, so they cannot photosynthesise.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Exercise 1: In the diagram comparing animal, plant and bacterial cells, where should 'Nucleoid' be written?
questions.explanation: The nucleoid is the feature unique to bacteria, which lack a true nucleus.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Exercise 1: Which label belongs in the region 'Common to all three cells'?
questions.explanation: All three have cytoplasm and a cell membrane. The nucleus is absent in bacteria, the cell wall is absent in animal cells, and chloroplasts are plant-only.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Exercise 1: Which part is present in both plant and bacterial cells but absent in animal cells?
questions.explanation: The cell wall is found in plant and bacterial cells (and fungi) but not animal cells. Chloroplasts are plant-only; the membrane is in all three.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Which is true of fungi but NOT of algae?
options: They lack chlorophyll and cannot make food
They are living things made up of cells
They can be made of more than one cell
They can live in soil as well as in water
questions.explanation: Algae contain chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis; fungi lack chloroplasts. Both are cellular, can be multicellular and live in soil or water.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Select ALL the statements that correctly describe differences between cell types.
options: Bacteria have a nucleoid, not a true nucleus
Viruses are made of a single cell
Animal cells have a cell wall
questions.explanation: Bacteria have a nucleoid and fungi lack chloroplasts. Viruses are acellular (no cell at all) and animal cells have no cell wall.

questions.topic: Comparing Cells: Bacteria, Fungi, Protozoa and Viruses
questions.question: Which microorganism cannot make its own food AND has a cell wall?
questions.explanation: Mould is a fungus: cell wall present, chloroplasts absent. Spirulina and Chlorella are microalgae that photosynthesise; Amoeba is a protozoan.
